puzzles.description: Why a coastline gets longer the more carefully you measure it, and what fractals have to do with it.
text: How long is the coastline of Great Britain? The question sounds [straightforward], yet it has no single correct answer. In fact, the more [meticulously] you measure it, the longer it seems to become.

The problem was famously [articulated] by the mathematician Benoit Mandelbrot in 1967, building on earlier work by the British scientist Lewis Fry Richardson. Richardson had noticed that [estimates] of the length of the same border varied wildly: Portugal, for instance, claimed that its border with Spain was considerably longer than the Spanish figure [suggested].

The explanation lies in the ruler. Measure the coast with a ruler 200 kilometres long, and you will [skip] over countless bays, inlets and headlands, arriving at a relatively modest figure. Shrink the ruler to 50 kilometres, and it begins to [trace] features that the longer one ignored, so the total grows. Reduce it to a metre, and every rock and [crevice] adds to the length. In principle, the figure [increases] without limit as the unit of measurement shrinks.

Coastlines, Mandelbrot argued, are [fractal]: they display similar patterns of [irregularity] at every scale, so zooming in never reveals a smooth line. Rather than asking how long a coast is, he suggested, we should describe how [rugged] it is.

Far from being a mere mathematical [curiosity], the paradox has practical [ramifications]. Official figures for a country's coastline can [diverge] dramatically depending on the map scale used, which matters when governments [allocate] funding for coastal defence or calculate the extent of their territorial waters. Published estimates for the coastline of the United States, for example, [differ] by more than a factor of three.

The paradox is a humbling [reminder] that even seemingly simple quantities are shaped by the choices we make when measuring them, and that precision, taken to its [extreme], can lead us not to certainty but to [infinity].

puzzles.description: A formal and gracious email turning down a job offer while keeping the door open for the future.
text: Dear Ms Whitfield,

Thank you very much for offering me the position of Senior Data Analyst at Northbridge Consulting, and for the time you and your colleagues [devoted] to the interview process. I was genuinely [impressed] by the team's expertise and by the openness with which you discussed the challenges ahead.

After a great deal of [deliberation], however, I have decided to [decline] the offer. This was by no means an easy decision. Shortly after our final interview, I received a [counteroffer] from my current employer that includes the opportunity to lead a new research unit, and I feel that this role is more closely [aligned] with my long-term goals.

I appreciate that this may cause some [inconvenience], particularly as you had hoped to fill the post before the end of the quarter, and I [apologise] for not being able to give you my answer sooner. I wanted to be certain that I was making the right choice rather than [rushing] into a commitment I might later regret.

I would also like to [reiterate] how much I enjoyed meeting the team. Our conversation about predictive modelling in healthcare was particularly [stimulating], and I left with a number of ideas I am still [mulling] over. Should an opportunity arise in the future that [matches] my experience, I would very much welcome the chance to be [considered].
In the meantime, I would be [delighted] to stay in touch, and if it would be of any [assistance], I would be happy to [recommend] a former colleague whose profile seems well [suited] to the position.
Thank you once again for your [generous] offer and for your understanding. I wish you and the team every [success] in the coming year.
Yours sincerely,
Tomás Ribeiro

puzzles.focus: Formal structures: the subjunctive and inverted conditionals
puzzles.rule: In formal English, verbs such as require, recommend, suggest and ask, and adjectives such as essential, vital or imperative, can be followed by that + the base form for every subject: it is essential that every student attend; the negative is not + base form (that attendance not fall). Conditionals can drop if and invert instead: should you need help (= if you need), were a student to fail (= if a student were to fail), had they applied (= if they had applied), were it not for (= without).
puzzles.description: Grammar focus: the subjunctive and inverted conditionals. A formal letter from a university confirming a place and setting out its conditions.
text: Dear Ms Oliveira,
We are delighted to confirm your place on the MSc in Environmental Policy, beginning on 22 September. Please read the following conditions carefully.

The University requires that all overseas students [be] registered with the International Office before the start of term. It is therefore essential that you [complete] the online enrolment form by 1 September and that your passport [be] presented in person during induction week. Please contact our admissions team [should] you experience any difficulty with the form.

Your offer remains conditional on the receipt of your final degree transcript. It is vital that the transcript [come] directly from your previous university, and we would be unable to confirm your enrolment [were] this document not to arrive by 15 August.

We strongly recommend that you [arrange] accommodation well in advance, and we would also suggest that you [open] a UK bank account as soon as you arrive. Many students last year would have been spared considerable stress [had] they [applied] for university housing before July.

Scholarship holders should note that the terms of the award stipulate that the recipient [maintain] an average grade of at least 60 per cent. It is equally imperative that attendance [not] fall below 80 per cent. Payments may be suspended [were] a student to fall below either threshold, although the committee will always consider [mitigating] circumstances. Were it not [for] the generosity of our alumni, many of these scholarships would not exist.

Finally, we ask that you [inform] us immediately [should] you decide not to take up your place, so that it can be offered to another [applicant]. Do not hesitate to get in touch [should] you require any further [information].
Yours sincerely,
Dr Helen Graham, Director of Admissions

puzzles.description: Cleopatra, mammoths and the fax machine: surprising overlaps that show how badly we picture historical time.
text: History is usually taught as a neat [sequence] of separate eras, which makes it easy to lose any intuitive [sense] of how events actually relate to one another in time. Consider a few examples that tend to [confound] our assumptions.

Cleopatra, the last active ruler of Ptolemaic Egypt, lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the construction of the Great Pyramid of Giza. By the time she was born, the pyramid was already around 2,500 years old and was itself an ancient [monument], marvelled at by Greek and Roman tourists.

Similarly, the woolly mammoth did not [vanish] as early as many people imagine. While most populations died out around 10,000 years ago, a small group [survived] on Wrangel Island, off the coast of Siberia, until roughly 4,000 years ago, several centuries after the Great Pyramid had been [completed].

Closer to the present, Oxford University was already teaching students more than two centuries before the Aztec city of Tenochtitlán was [founded]. And the fax machine, which most of us [associate] with offices in the 1980s, was first [patented] in 1843, the same year that large wagon trains set out along the Oregon Trail, and decades before the telephone was [invented].

Such [juxtapositions] are more than party trivia. They [expose] the way our mental timeline tends to [compress] the distant past into a single, blurry “long ago”, while [stretching] out the recent past in considerable detail. They also remind us that history does not [unfold] at the same pace everywhere: technologies, institutions and ways of life that seem [incompatible] often coexisted for centuries.

Perhaps the most [sobering] lesson is how short recorded history really is. If the entire history of the Earth were [condensed] into a single day, the whole of human civilisation would [occupy] less than the final second before midnight.

puzzles.description: How to handle networking events: breaking the ice, listening well, ending a conversation and managing expectations.
text: For many professionals, walking into a room full of strangers at a networking event is [daunting]. The drinks are lukewarm, the name badges are [illegible], and everyone else seems to know exactly what to say. Yet small talk is a skill like any other, and, with a little [practice], it can be [honed].

The first step is to [abandon] the idea that you need to impress. Most people are far more [preoccupied] with how they themselves come across than with judging you. Approaching someone who is standing alone is usually the easiest way to [break] the ice; they are likely to be [relieved] that somebody has made the first move.

Open with a remark about your shared [surroundings] rather than a question about someone's job title. A comment on the venue or the talk you have both just heard is less [intrusive] and gives the other person an easy way in. From there, open-ended questions tend to [yield] more interesting conversations than those that can be answered with a simple yes or no.

Listening is at least as important as talking. Resist the [temptation] to plan your next contribution while the other person is still speaking, and pick up on [details] they mention in passing: these are often the key to a more memorable exchange. By the same token, don't [monopolise] the conversation with a detailed account of your own career.

Knowing how to end a conversation is equally [valuable]. There is nothing [rude] about saying that you have enjoyed talking and would like to meet a few more people before the evening is over. If the exchange has been fruitful, suggest a concrete way to [follow] up, such as sending an article you discussed.

Finally, keep your [expectations] realistic. Not every conversation will lead to a job offer or a new client, and that is perfectly fine. The real [payoff] of networking often comes months later, when a casual acquaintance [remembers] you at exactly the right moment.

puzzles.theme: What Nobody Tells You About Marathons
puzzles.rule: Cleft sentences split one idea into two parts to put the focus on the most important information: What surprised me was…, It was my sister who convinced me…, It wasn't the long runs that exhausted me…, All I could think about was…, The reason why…, The place where… You can also stress a verb with do, does or did + base form: I did finish.
puzzles.description: Grammar focus: cleft sentences and emphatic do. A first-time runner describes the surprises of training for and running a marathon.
text: Last April, I ran my first marathon. People had warned me about the pain and the early mornings, but there were several things [that] nobody mentioned, and what [surprised] me most [was] how emotional the whole experience would be.

It was actually my sister [who] convinced me to sign up. She had run the Rio de Janeiro Marathon two years earlier, and the thing [that] impressed me [wasn't] her finishing time but the way she talked about the crowd.

The training was tough, I [do] admit. What I hadn't expected, though, [was] that the hardest part would be mental rather than physical. It wasn't the long runs [that] exhausted me; [it] was the constant negotiation with myself at five o'clock in the morning.

On race day, the reason [why] I kept going after the thirtieth kilometre was simple: all I [could] think about [was] the finish line. The place [where] I nearly gave up was a long, empty stretch of road with nobody cheering.

What [kept] me moving [was] a complete stranger. An elderly man at the side of the road shouted my name, which was printed on my race number, and it was [then] that I realised how much encouragement from others matters.
I [did] finish, in four hours and thirty-seven minutes. Where I celebrated afterwards [was] a small café near the finish line, and what I [ordered] was the biggest plate of pasta I have ever eaten.

puzzles.description: In 1932, the Australian army sent machine guns against 20,000 emus. The emus won.
text: In late 1932, the Australian government went to war against an unlikely [adversary]: the emu. The conflict, which has since become the stuff of internet legend, ended in what many observers [regarded] as a humiliating defeat for the soldiers.

The trouble began after the First World War, when thousands of former soldiers were given land in Western Australia to farm wheat. Their situation was already [precarious]: the Great Depression had sent wheat prices [plummeting], and promised government subsidies had failed to [materialise]. Then, after the breeding season, some 20,000 emus [descended] on the region, trampling crops and tearing holes in the fences that kept out rabbits.

The farmers [appealed] to the Minister of Defence, who agreed to send a small military [detachment] armed with two Lewis machine guns and 10,000 rounds of ammunition. The operation, led by Major G. P. W. Meredith, was expected to be [swift].

It proved anything but. The emus, it turned out, were remarkably adept at [evading] gunfire. At the first sign of danger, the flocks would [scatter] in all directions, making them almost impossible to target. On one occasion, the soldiers laid an [ambush] near a dam, but the gun jammed after only a dozen birds had been killed. Mounting a machine gun on a truck fared no better, as the vehicle could not keep [pace] with the birds over rough ground.

Meredith later [remarked] that if he had a military division with the bullet-carrying capacity of these birds, it would face any army in the world. After a month of [sporadic] fighting, and amid growing [ridicule] in the press, the soldiers were [withdrawn]. The government [subsequently] turned to a bounty system, which proved considerably more effective.
Whether the episode truly counts as a defeat is open to debate, but it has [endured] as a wry reminder that nature does not always [yield] to brute force.

puzzles.description: Friends at a book club debate a slow start, a twist ending and an unreliable narrator, full of idiomatic English.
text: Laura: So, what did everyone make of it? I have to [confess], I couldn't put it down.
Miguel: Really? I found it hard [going], to be honest. The first hundred pages were so slow that I nearly [gave] up.
Laura: I know what you mean, but the slow start [rewards] your patience. By the time you get to the flood, you're completely [invested] in the characters.
Aisha: I'm with Laura on this one. But what struck me most was the ending. I didn't see that twist [coming] at all.
Miguel: Didn't you? I thought it was [telegraphed] from the very first chapter. The moment the brother mentioned the letter, I had a [hunch] it would come back.
Aisha: Well, you've always had a knack for spotting plot twists. Some of us just go with the [flow].
Laura: Can I play devil's [advocate] for a moment? Some reviewers said the narrator was completely [unreliable], and that nothing she tells us about her mother should be taken at face [value].
Miguel: I'd go even further. I think the author deliberately [muddies] the waters so that we never quite know whose version to believe.
Aisha: That's a fair [point], but isn't that a bit of a [cop-out]? At some stage, you have to give readers something solid to hold on to.
Laura: Maybe. Either way, it certainly got us talking. Shall we [move] on to next month's book?
Miguel: Please tell me it's shorter. I'm not sure I can [face] another five hundred pages.
Aisha: It's a collection of short stories, so you're [off] the hook.
Miguel: Thank goodness. Right, whose turn is it to [host]?
Laura: Yours, I'm [afraid]. And you promised to bake.

puzzles.rule: To report beliefs and claims without saying who holds them, use it + passive reporting verb + that (it was revealed that…) or subject + passive reporting verb + to-infinitive (Nessie is said to be…). For earlier events, use the perfect infinitive to have + past participle (believed to have died out), and to have been + past participle in the passive (supposed to have been taken). For actions in progress, use to be + -ing (rumoured to be waiting).
puzzles.description: Grammar focus: passive reporting structures (is said to be, is believed to have…). Legends, hoaxes and DNA tests at Loch Ness.
text: Loch Ness, in the Scottish Highlands, is said [to] be home to one of the world's most famous monsters. The creature, affectionately known as Nessie, is thought to [be] a large, long-necked animal resembling a plesiosaur, a marine reptile generally believed to [have] died out 66 million years ago.

Sightings are claimed to [go] back as far as the sixth century, when Saint Columba is reported to have [driven] a “water beast” back into the River Ness. The modern legend, however, is usually considered to have [begun] in 1933, when a new road along the northern shore gave motorists a clear view of the water.

The most famous image of Nessie, the so-called Surgeon's Photograph of 1934, was long supposed to have [been] taken by a respected London doctor. In 1994, however, [it] was revealed [that] the picture was a hoax: the “monster” was a toy submarine [fitted] with a head made of wood putty.

Despite this, the loch continues to attract thousands of hopeful visitors, and dozens of new sightings [are] reported every year. It has been [estimated] that Nessie-related tourism is worth around £40 million a year to the Scottish economy.

In 2018, a team of scientists analysed the DNA [left] behind in the water by the creatures living in the loch. No reptile DNA was found, but there were large quantities of eel DNA, and it has since been suggested that people may have [been] mistaking unusually large eels for a monster. Eels [are] not known to grow to the size described in many sightings, but the theory is considered far more [plausible] than the survival of a prehistoric reptile.

Whether Nessie exists or not, she is unlikely [to] disappear from the popular imagination. Somewhere in the loch, she is rumoured to be [waiting] for the next eager tourist with a camera, and she is believed to [have] been [seen] again only last summer.

puzzles.theme: Why English Spelling Is So Strange
puzzles.description: Flemish printers, the Great Vowel Shift and Renaissance scholars: how English spelling became so irregular.
text: Few aspects of English cause learners, and native speakers, as much [frustration] as its spelling. Why do “though”, “through”, “tough” and “cough” look so similar yet sound so different? The answer lies in a long and rather [haphazard] history.

Much of the [inconsistency] dates back to the fifteenth century. When William Caxton set up England's first printing press in 1476, spelling had not yet been [standardised], and many of his typesetters came from Flanders. Unfamiliar with English, they sometimes [imposed] Flemish conventions: the “h” in “ghost”, for instance, is widely [attributed] to their influence.

At roughly the same time, the language was undergoing a [dramatic] change in pronunciation known as the Great Vowel Shift. Over two or three centuries, the long vowels gradually [shifted] upwards in the mouth, so that “bite”, once pronounced rather like “beet”, acquired its modern sound. Unfortunately, printing had begun to [fix] spellings just as pronunciation was changing, leaving written English [stranded] somewhere in the past.

Later scholars made matters worse. During the Renaissance, some writers, eager to [display] their classical learning, inserted silent letters to [reflect] a word's Latin origin. The “b” in “debt” was added because of the Latin debitum, even though the word had [entered] English from French without it. In some cases, the scholars were simply [mistaken]: the “s” in “island” comes from a false association with the Latin insula, although the word is in fact of Germanic origin. English has also [borrowed] freely from other languages, often keeping the original spelling, as in “ballet”, “yacht” and “psychology”.

Numerous reformers, from Benjamin Franklin to George Bernard Shaw, have [campaigned] for a more phonetic system, but none has succeeded. Any reform would render centuries of printed text [obsolete], and, given the variety of accents across the English-speaking world, it is far from clear whose pronunciation a new system should [mirror]. Paradoxically, the very quirks that make English spelling so [maddening] also [preserve] a fascinating record of the language's past.
